candidates.quote: But when the laws are written down, rich and weak alike have equal justice.
candidates.author: Euripides
candidates.locator: lines 433 to 435, Theseus answering the Theban herald; verified on Perseus in Coleridge's English, where the sentence runs on, so the full stop marks a cut at a complete clause
candidates.speaker: Theseus
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the oldest plain statement of what justice is for: written law so that the weak can answer the rich in the same words.

candidates.quote: Terrible is the temptation to do good!
candidates.author: Bertolt Brecht
candidates.locator: scene 2, The Flight into the Northern Mountains, the Singer as Grusha takes up the child; HEDGE: the Bentley page was not opened, so the wording and the scene number rest on secondary citation and must be checked against Parables for the Theatre
candidates.speaker: the Singer
candidates.whyThisMonth: It names the cost of service honestly at six in the morning: helping is a temptation you pay for, and Grusha pays and does it anyway.

candidates.quote: I shall always be a flower girl to Professor Higgins, because he always treats me as a flower girl, and always will; but I know I can be a lady to you, because you always treat me as a lady, and always will.
candidates.author: Bernard Shaw
candidates.locator: Act V, Liza to Colonel Pickering, in the speech on the difference between a lady and a flower girl; this sentence chosen over the famous one before it because it carries no contraction and so no risk from Shaw's apostrophe practice
candidates.speaker: Liza Doolittle
candidates.whyThisMonth: What is owed to a person is not admiration but treatment, and Liza shows that the treatment makes the person.

candidates.quote: Sometimes I think it ain’t right to stand and watch them do it.
candidates.author: Lillian Hellman
candidates.locator: Act III, the close of Addie's speech on those who eat the earth; Hellman herself called it the third act speech that carries the burden of the play, in her Paris Review interview
candidates.speaker: Addie
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month's hardest question in a servant's plain words: not what the greedy owe, but what the watchers owe.

candidates.quote: Yes, I’d give the Devil benefit of law, for my own safety’s sake.
candidates.author: Robert Bolt
candidates.locator: Act One, More to Roper, the closing sentence of the speech on the laws planted thick from coast to coast; chosen because it is the one sentence of that speech with no em dash in it
candidates.speaker: Sir Thomas More
candidates.whyThisMonth: Justice is not a favour done to the deserving: More keeps the law for the Devil because that is the only way it stands for him too.

candidates.quote: Attention, attention must be finally paid to such a person.
candidates.author: Arthur Miller
candidates.locator: Act One, Linda to her sons, in the speech beginning I don't say he's a great man; Viking Press, 1949
candidates.speaker: Linda Loman
candidates.whyThisMonth: The smallest thing anyone is owed, and the one most often withheld: notice taken of an ordinary person.

candidates.quote: Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free, / The wretched refuse of your teeming shore. / Send these, the homeless, tempest-tost to me, / I lift my lamp beside the golden door!
candidates.author: Emma Lazarus
candidates.locator: lines 10 to 14, the sonnet's closing, spoken by the Mother of Exiles; The Poems of Emma Lazarus, vol. I, p. 202 (Houghton Mifflin, 1889); the poem encloses these lines in quotation marks, which the card drops
candidates.speaker: the Mother of Exiles
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the welcome as a duty rather than a kindness, and it is the line the month's theme was made for.

candidates.quote: For there is no friend like a sister / In calm or stormy weather; / To cheer one on the tedious way, / To fetch one if one goes astray, / To lift one if one totters down, / To strengthen whilst one stands.
candidates.author: Christina Rossetti
candidates.locator: the closing lines, Laura to the children, Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862); the poem prints them inside single quotation marks, which the card drops
candidates.speaker: Laura
candidates.whyThisMonth: Four verbs for what one person owes another: cheer, fetch, lift, strengthen, and none of them abstract.

candidates.quote: To sin by silence, when we should protest, / Makes cowards out of men. The human race / Has climbed on protest.
candidates.author: Ella Wheeler Wilcox
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 3, the opening; Poems of Problems (W. B. Conkey, 1914), and the 1914 collection title rests on secondary sources, though the year is firm
candidates.whyThisMonth: It turns silence from a neutral thing into a debt unpaid, and it does it in three lines before breakfast.

candidates.quote: Let a new earth rise. Let another world be born.
candidates.author: Margaret Walker
candidates.locator: the opening of the final stanza, For My People (Yale University Press, 1942); the poem's long Whitmanic lines are set as blocks, so these two sentences sit inside one printed line and take no slash
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month needs one line that asks for everything rather than a little more fairness, and this is it.

candidates.quote: Your fault beeing greater, why should you disdaine / Our beeing your equals, free from tyranny?
candidates.author: Aemilia Lanyer
candidates.locator: Eves Apologie in defence of Women, the stanza beginning Then let us have our Libertie againe (1611); HEDGE: the line numbers, usually given in the 820s, were not confirmed against Susanne Woods's Oxford edition of 1993, and many anthologies modernise beeing to being
candidates.whyThisMonth: The first Englishwoman to publish a book of poems asks for equality as a debt, not a gift, and asks it as a question.

candidates.quote: Yes, injured Woman! rise, assert thy right!
candidates.author: Anna Laetitia Barbauld
candidates.locator: the opening line; written about 1792 in answer to Wollstonecraft and first printed in The Works of Anna Lætitia Barbauld, ed. Lucy Aikin, vol. I (Longman, 1825); the poem's last stanza turns and qualifies the call
candidates.whyThisMonth: A summons rather than a plea, and short enough to carry all day.

candidates.quote: Music to soothe all its sorrow, / Till war and crime shall cease; / And the hearts of men grown tender / Girdle the world with peace.
candidates.author: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper
candidates.locator: the closing stanza; Poems (George S. Ferguson, 1896), the text carried by the Academy of American Poets, which is also printed in the Atlanta Offering of 1895
candidates.whyThisMonth: A poet who lectured for a living asks what her work is for, and answers: other people.

candidates.quote: The sons of Adam are limbs of each other / Having been created of one essence. / When the calamity of time afflicts one limb / The other limbs cannot remain at rest.
candidates.author: Saadi
candidates.locator: chapter I, On the Conduct of Kings, story 10, the Bani Adam verse, lines 1 to 4; Rehatsek's version was completed in 1888 and reprinted in 1928 under Richard Burton's name
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest argument for the debt to strangers: one body, so one limb's trouble is every limb's.

candidates.quote: Thinking of this, secretly I grew ashamed; / And all day the thought lingered in my head.
candidates.author: Bai Juyi
candidates.locator: the closing two lines, poem 15 of the Po Chü-i section, More Translations from the Chinese (Alfred A. Knopf, 1919); Waley dates the poem A.D. 806 and prints the poet's name as Po Chü-i
candidates.whyThisMonth: A salaried official watches people work in the heat and cannot get past his own comfort: the exact shame the month is for.

candidates.quote: From the place where we are right / flowers will never grow / in the spring.
candidates.author: Yehuda Amichai
candidates.work: The Place Where We Are Right
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 3, the opening; The Selected Poetry of Yehuda Amichai (Harper and Row, 1986; University of California Press from 1996); the Hebrew original's first publication date was not confirmed
candidates.whyThisMonth: Justice starts by loosening the ground under your own certainty, which is the kindest thing to be told at six in the morning.
